_about: Per card: provenance (where the card came from), refs (works its source line names), see_also (published works an AI agent matched to "design practice" cards afterwards and a second blind check confirmed; supporting reading, not the source). Works are in data/references.json.

see_also.why: Lynch's image of the city (paths, edges, nodes, landmarks) directly matches using the moat as an edge, gates as nodes/checkpoints and bastions as landmarks on a loop route.
Reeves et al. specifically address designing for spectators who watch players perform in public, including how to make the player's experience visible and understandable to onlookers.
Reeves et al. discuss how spectators see the player's body and manipulations rather than the game state, so performances should be designed with audience visibility in mind.
Reeves et al. cover designing the spectator experience including the physical relationship between performers and audience in public game settings.
Reeves et al. focus on evaluating spectator engagement and experience, matching these playtest questions about audience reactions and involvement.

Bruckman argues educational value comes from integrating learning into the activity itself, matching the card's idea that students learn by designing and justifying the game rather than just playing it.
The card explicitly invokes submission, one of MDA's eight aesthetics, describing removal of pressure mechanics to achieve it.
Game Accessibility Guidelines cover cognitive accessibility including predictable, low-overload presentation for sensitive players.
Movement-Based Game Guidelines address exertion, fatigue and rest in movement games, matching the set/rest interval structure.
Movement-Based Game Guidelines discuss fatigue and bodily limits in exertion play, matching break and heat guidance.
Meta's health and safety guidance covers play area, breaks and supervision for active headset use.
Koster's fun-as-mastery of patterns matches designing a repeatable skill that grows with practice runs.
Reeves et al. cover designing the spectator experience, matching the final as a spectator moment with crowd-side portals.
Game Accessibility Guidelines cover motor accessibility, matching the wide-route, gentle-turn design for wheelchair players.
Game Accessibility Guidelines cover motor accessibility and alternative input, matching full seated play options.
Game Accessibility Guidelines cover vision accessibility and colour-blind safe palettes, matching the hazard contrast advice.
WCAG covers contrast ratios and non-colour-only cues, matching the red-hazard-on-neutral-ground contrast rule.
Game Accessibility Guidelines cover cognitive accessibility including clear, simple language in game text.
Movement-Based Game Guidelines directly address exertion, fatigue, and safety in movement games, matching the card's effort and near-miss measures.
Game Accessibility Guidelines cover motor and cognitive access so that every player, including youngest/oldest and those needing aides, can finish.
Meta's mixed reality guidelines discuss room boundaries and real walls, which the card turns into deliberate world edges.
Designing the Spectator Experience directly addresses how spectators and visible performance shape play in public settings.
Meta's safety guidance covers play area supervision and adult oversight, matching the card's spotter role for group play.
Juul's Half-Real argues rules gain meaning through fiction, supporting the idea that a time limit (rule) needs a story reason (fiction) to feel like tension rather than a test.
Reeves et al. on designing the spectator experience directly covers making manipulations and effects visible so onlookers (here, parents watching and calling out) can join the play.
Bruckman's 'chocolate-covered broccoli' argument says learning must be integrated into play rather than bolted on, matching the card's rule that the story carries the lesson as a mission, not a test.
Malone's theory of intrinsically motivating instruction grounds the card's use of fantasy missions and curiosity to carry short true facts in learning games.
The MDA framework names 'submission' as an aesthetic, and the card is about writing text that supports exactly that aesthetic (calm verbs, no threats or clocks).
MDA lists 'discovery' as an aesthetic, and the card's hint-don't-spoil labeling is a technique for delivering that aesthetic without spoiling surprises.
MDA names 'sensation' as an aesthetic, and the card prescribes punchy sensory text paired with strong visuals to serve it.
Lynch's Image of the City defines landmarks as orienting elements that pull navigation, exactly the card's visible-goal-from-spawn technique.
Jenkins' narrative architecture describes environmental storytelling where the space itself evokes narrative, which is what mapping the real room into the fiction accomplishes.
Schell's interest curves lens describes building experience toward peaks, matching the card's small-sights-then-one-big-reveal structure for wonder.
Freytag's dramatic arc of rising action to climax underpins the card's rule of raising stakes one step per chapter rather than opening at maximum.

Luminate discusses structured exploration of a design space with LLMs generating diverse options along dimensions, matching the card's approach of offering distinct theme options to resolve an open brief.
CLAM directly addresses asking a clarifying question only when an ambiguous request has genuinely divergent interpretations.
CLAM's clarifying-question approach matches asking 'Chill like...?' to disambiguate the word's readings.
